newsitem.title: UK: Russia shrugs off past with Eurobond success.
newsitem.headline: Russia shrugs off past with Eurobond success.

text.p: Just seven years after the fall of the Berlin Wall, huge demand for Russia's debut Eurobond shows how closely the country has integrated with the world's capital markets and how fast perceptions of economic and political risk can change.
The lead managers for the issue said on Thursday Russia had raised $1.0 billion, double original expectations, via a five-year offering at 345 basis points over U.S. Treasuries.

"This is a huge economy, even at prevailing exchange rates it is worth $360 billion and at purchasing power parity is the sixth largest country in the world in terms of gross domestic product," said Jonathan Hoffman, head of emerging market research at CS First Boston in London.

The Eurobond is Russia's first entry into western capital markets since the 1917 revolution, and comes a month after RAO Gazprom, the world's largest natural gas producer, raised $430 million from overseas investors in a deal which was five times oversubscribed.

"Certain classes of investors had been excluded from Russia because of the rules governing their funds. Now with the development of euroclearable instruments, these people can get into the market," said Philip Poole head of emerging market economics at ING Barings in London.

Russian Brady debt, currently being restructured, rose to 80 percent of face value in early trade in London. But the main beneficiaries of the Eurobond's success were MinFin bonds, which surged up to three quarters of a point to 83 3/4 percent.
"There is good scope to see Russian debt tighten in the wake of this issue, especially in the MinFins," said ING's Poole.
Paul Luke, head of emerging debt research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said that at 345 basis points over U.S. Treasuries, the eurobond is discounting a default risk of around 15 percent.
"There is no doubt that the Russians will pay and in reality there is no risk of default," he said.
However, there may yet be some hiccoughs in Russia's parade through the world's capital markets.

President Boris Yeltsin's health remains an issue. Alexander Lebed, the former general ousted from his post of security chief in October, is still popular in Russia. And chief of staff Anatoly Chubais has been criticised by the opposition for accumulating too much power during Yeltsin's illness.
"It is always thus in Russia, three steps forward, one back. But the Eurobond is a huge leap forward," said CS First Boston's Hoffman.

As well as Russia's murky politics, the country has still not received the October tranche of a $10.2 billion loan from the International Monetary Fund because of poor levels of tax collection, which have imperilled the country's budgetary plans. "Sure, there is plenty of scope for things to go wrong, but if you look at the economy, inflation is declining, external debt is very low and the country is running a healthy trade surplus," said ING's Poole.
Most analysts expect the IMF to resume its payments and note that tax collection, which had been running at 60 percent of its target, has risen sharply.
"Russia is as important to the IMF and the wider international community as the IMF is to Russia. Neither side can walk away," said Poole.
